dek: Carbonite let ordinary people stop worrying about a dead hard drive, for one flat yearly price.
lede: Carbonite became one of the most familiar voices on American talk radio by selling something most listeners had never thought to buy: backup. For a flat yearly price, its software copied everything on a home computer to servers in a data center. A dead hard drive or a stolen laptop no longer meant lost photos and tax returns. By the summer of 2011, broadband was everywhere and the cloud was a household word.

sections.heading: Ads for Non-Techies
sections.body: David Friend and Jeff Flowers were serial founders from the Boston tech scene. They bet that ordinary people would pay a small subscription to never think about backup again. Most consumers had no backup at all. Carbonite made it automatic and unlimited. Then it spent heavily on radio and podcast ads to reach people who would never read a tech review. Later it added plans for small businesses, and those customers proved steadier.

sections.heading: From Living Rooms to Webroot
sections.body: Carbonite priced its IPO at $10 a share in August 2011, in a jittery market. The stock traded unevenly for years as consumer growth slowed. So the company turned toward business customers and bought several rivals. The biggest name among them was Webroot, in 2019. Later that same year, OpenText agreed to buy Carbonite for about $1.42 billion and folded it into its enterprise software group.

tagline: A Price Tag on Every House
dek: Zillow let anyone see what a home was worth, including their own and their neighbor's.
lede: Zillow put a number on nearly every home in America, including the ones nobody was selling. That number, the Zestimate, sat beside listings and sales histories for tens of millions of homes. When Zillow filed to go public in 2011, housing was still deep in the wreckage of the financial crisis. People kept looking anyway, often at their own homes and their neighbors'. Zillow had become one of the most visited real estate sites in the country.

sections.heading: From Expedia to Housing
sections.body: Rich Barton had already turned travel booking into a consumer product at Expedia. With Lloyd Frink, he bet that real estate data could be opened up to everyone. Agents and listing services had long held it close. The Zestimate, launched in 2006, was the hook: a free, instant number for any address, and one people loved to argue over. Zillow made its money from agents and advertisers who wanted to reach all those curious browsers.

sections.heading: Trulia, Then a Costly Detour
sections.body: Zillow priced its IPO at $20 a share in July 2011 and traded well above that on its first day. In 2015 it bought its rival Trulia and became the dominant home search site in the United States. Then it tried buying and flipping homes itself. That business, Zillow Offers, ended in 2021 with large losses. Zillow went back to running a marketplace, and it remains publicly traded.

dek: HomeAway let families find a beach house or a cabin for the week without a stack of classified ads.
lede: HomeAway built the world's largest vacation rental marketplace mostly by buying other people's websites. Before it, renting a beach house meant classified ads, phone calls and word of mouth. HomeAway bought up listing sites such as VRBO and gathered them in one place. Owners paid to advertise their homes, and travelers browsed for free. When it filed to go public in 2011, Airbnb was still a young startup.

sections.heading: An Austin Shopping Spree
sections.body: Brian Sharples and Carl Shepherd started in Austin in 2005 with a roll-up plan. They raised a large amount of venture money early. They spent it on established rental sites in the United States and Europe, including VRBO. The model was simple. Owners paid a yearly subscription to list their properties, and travelers searched for free. More listings drew more travelers, and more travelers drew more owners.

sections.heading: Renamed for Vrbo
sections.body: HomeAway priced its IPO at $27 a share in June 2011 and closed its first day well above that. Over the next few years, Airbnb grew into a serious rival. HomeAway answered by charging travelers a booking fee. In 2015 Expedia bought HomeAway for about $3.9 billion. The business later took the name of one of the oldest sites it had bought: Vrbo.

cover.theme: a fisherman's cottage by the water (a vacation home)

dek: LinkedIn let people keep their résumé online, so the next job could come looking for them.
lede: LinkedIn went public a year ahead of Facebook, and Wall Street treated its listing as a test of the whole social media wave. It was the first major American social network to sell shares. Its members kept an online record of their careers and connected with colleagues. Recruiters paid to search that map of the working world. By 2011 LinkedIn had more than 100 million members.

sections.heading: Friends From PayPal
sections.body: Reid Hoffman, an early PayPal executive, started LinkedIn with a small group of friends from SocialNet and PayPal. They launched it in 2003. The bet was that professionals would put their real names and work histories online if the network got them jobs and deals. LinkedIn made money three ways: recruiting tools, advertising and premium subscriptions. Recruiting became the engine that drove the rest.

sections.heading: Microsoft's Biggest Check
sections.body: LinkedIn priced its shares at $45 in May 2011 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock more than doubled on its first day of trading. LinkedIn grew steadily as a public company and bought Lynda.com in 2015. A year later, Microsoft bought LinkedIn for $26.2 billion, its largest purchase up to then. Microsoft kept LinkedIn running as an independent brand.

tagline: The Name at the Airport Gate
dek: Boingo got travelers online at the airport gate, then built wireless networks for stadiums and military bases.
lede: When a traveler opened a laptop at an airport gate, the name on the screen was often Boingo. The company ran paid Wi-Fi in many of the busiest airports in the United States and resold access to hotspots around the world. By 2011 smartphones were changing the business. Boingo was also building cellular antenna systems inside airports and stadiums, so phone carriers could serve the crowds there.

sections.heading: After EarthLink, One Login
sections.body: Sky Dayton had founded the internet provider EarthLink. He started Boingo in 2001, when public Wi-Fi was new and scattered. His bet was that one account could work across thousands of hotspots, the way a phone worked across cell towers. Boingo won long contracts to run the networks in major airports. Roaming deals with other hotspot operators let its customers log in far beyond its own locations.

sections.heading: When Wi-Fi Went Free
sections.body: Boingo priced its IPO at $13.50 a share in May 2011. Then free Wi-Fi spread through airports and coffee shops. The company leaned into building wireless infrastructure for venues, carriers and military bases. Its long airport contracts and base networks kept revenue steady as consumer Wi-Fi fees faded. In 2021 an investment group led by Digital Colony bought Boingo and took it private.

cover.theme: kites in the sky (signals in the air)
cover.artwork: Kites of Fukuroi and Distant View of Akiba in Totomi Province (Enshu Akiba enkei Fukuroi tako), from the series "One Hundred Famous Views in the Various Provinces (Shokoku meisho hyakkei)"

tagline: The Mortgage Leaves the Fax Machine
dek: Ellie Mae let lenders close home loans in software instead of by fax and courier.
lede: Ellie Mae went public in 2011 with a business built on mortgages, at a moment when few investors wanted anything to do with them. Housing was still recovering from the crash. Ellie Mae's software sat behind the loan. Its Encompass system let lenders and brokers take in an application, check it, price it and close it. Its network connected them to the appraisers, credit bureaus and investors involved in every loan.

sections.heading: Loans by Fax and Courier
sections.body: Sig Anderman and Limin Hu started the company in 1997, when a mortgage still traveled by fax and courier. They bet that loan origination could move onto one shared platform. Lenders would pay per loan to use it. Ellie Mae won its first customers among small and midsize lenders. Larger lenders signed on later, as regulation made careful records essential.

sections.heading: From $6 to $11 Billion
sections.body: Ellie Mae priced its IPO at $6 a share in April 2011, below its planned range. It listed on the NYSE Amex exchange. Then refinancing and new rules drove lenders to its software, and the stock rose many times over. Thoma Bravo took the company private in 2019 for about $3.7 billion. A year later, Intercontinental Exchange bought Ellie Mae for about $11 billion.

cover.theme: a doorway (the way into a home)

dek: GAIN Capital let ordinary people trade dollars, euros and yen from home, at any hour.
lede: GAIN Capital let people trade the world's currencies from a home computer, with borrowed money, around the clock. Through FOREX.com and other platforms, customers bet on dollars, euros and yen with low minimums. By late 2010, retail forex was a fast-growing corner of finance that few people understood. New American rules were just starting to cap leverage and tighten oversight. GAIN was one of the largest brokers in the field.

sections.heading: A Trading Floor, Repackaged
sections.body: Mark Galant founded GAIN in 1999 with a simple idea. The professional foreign exchange market could be packaged for individuals online. GAIN took the other side of many customer trades and earned money from the spread between buying and selling prices. Retail forex was young and loosely regulated. GAIN grew in the United States, then expanded into the United Kingdom, Japan and other markets.

sections.heading: A Decade Under $9
sections.body: GAIN priced its IPO at $9 a share in December 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. To grow, it bought rivals including GFT and City Index. Tighter regulation and calm currency markets weighed on the business. Its shares spent most of the next decade below the offering price. In 2020 INTL FCStone bought GAIN and renamed itself StoneX.

dek: Envestnet gave independent financial advisers the tools the big brokerages had, so they could compete on their own.
lede: Envestnet built the back office for financial advisers who quit the big brokerages. Its platform let an adviser open accounts, build portfolios from many outside managers, rebalance them and report to clients, all in one place. Those were the tools the big firms had always provided. As more advisers went independent, they needed someone else to supply them. Envestnet filed to go public in the summer of 2010, as markets recovered from the crisis.

sections.heading: Fees Over Commissions
sections.body: Judson Bergman started Envestnet in 1999 with a bet on the independent adviser. He saw wealth management moving away from commissions and toward fee-based accounts. Advisers would pay for technology that made those accounts run. Envestnet charged a small fee on the assets on its platform, so it grew as markets and its adviser base grew. Its open design let advisers pick from many outside money managers, which set it apart from captive brokerage platforms.

sections.heading: Yodlee and the Data Trove
sections.body: Envestnet priced its IPO at $9 a share in July 2010 and listed on the New York Stock Exchange. It grew through acquisitions. One was the data business Yodlee, in 2015, which brought a large store of financial account data that Envestnet sold to banks and fintech companies. Assets on its platform rose into the trillions of dollars. In 2024 Bain Capital took Envestnet private in a deal valued at about $4.5 billion.

cover.theme: a harvest field (wealth grown over time)

dek: ReachLocal got plumbers, dentists and restaurants found on Google without making them learn how search ads work.
lede: ReachLocal sent a large sales force door to door to sell Google ads to plumbers, dentists and restaurants. These owners knew their customers searched online. Few of them knew how to buy a search ad. ReachLocal's salespeople signed them up. Its software then spread each budget across search engines and tracked the calls that came back. In 2010 the company was growing fast across the United States and abroad.

sections.heading: One Budget, No Homework
sections.body: Zorik Gordon and Michael Kline founded ReachLocal in 2004. They bet that small businesses would pay a premium to hand their online advertising to someone else. The pitch was simple: the owner paid one monthly budget, and ReachLocal handled the rest. The company built a large sales force and its own campaign software. It earned its margin on the gap between what clients paid and what the media cost.

sections.heading: When Ads Went Self-Serve
sections.body: ReachLocal priced its IPO at $13 a share in May 2010. Over time, Google and Facebook made self-serve advertising easy for even the smallest shops. Small businesses found cheaper ways to advertise, and the costly sales force became a burden. Revenue fell, and the stock sank far below its offering price. In 2016 the newspaper publisher Gannett bought ReachLocal for about $156 million.

cover.theme: a busy street of shops (local business)

dek: Convio let charities collect donations, send email and stay close to supporters over the internet.
lede: Convio's signature product let people sign up for a charity walk or run and raise money from their friends online. That was one piece of a larger hosted service. Convio ran donation pages, email campaigns, event registrations and donor databases for nonprofits, from local food banks to national health charities. By 2010 online giving grew every year. Charities were learning to treat their websites as a front door for supporters.

sections.heading: Retail Tools for Food Banks
sections.body: Convio started in Austin in 1999. Its bet was that nonprofits would need the same online tools retailers were adopting, and could not build them alone. It sold its software as a subscription service, years before that model was common. Beyond the charity walks, its tools let groups keep in touch with donors between campaigns, through email newsletters and online advocacy.

sections.heading: Folded Into Luminate
sections.body: Convio priced its IPO at $9 a share in April 2010. It grew modestly as a public company in a market led by Blackbaud, the larger nonprofit software maker. In 2012 Blackbaud agreed to buy Convio for about $275 million. The deal joined the two best-known names in nonprofit software. Blackbaud kept parts of the Convio platform, and they became the base of its Luminate products for large nonprofits.

cover.artwork: New York Charities—St Barnabas House, 304 Mulberry Street

dek: Financial Engines told workers how to invest their 401(k) savings, and for a fee managed the money itself.
lede: Financial Engines had a Nobel Prize winner among its founders, and it sold his kind of finance to people saving in a 401(k). Workers got advice on how to invest their retirement money. For a fee, the company would manage those accounts for them. It sold through employers and plan providers instead of directly to the public. When it filed in early 2010, the crisis had just wiped out much of many workers' savings.

sections.heading: Portfolio Theory for Everyone
sections.body: William Sharpe won the Nobel Prize in economics in 1990. In 1996 he co-founded the company with securities law professor Joseph Grundfest and venture capitalist Craig Johnson. Their bet was that rigorous portfolio models could reach millions of ordinary savers cheaply over the internet. Then Congress opened the door wider. The Pension Protection Act of 2006 encouraged automatic advice in retirement plans.

sections.heading: First Out After the Crash
sections.body: Financial Engines priced its IPO at $12 a share in March 2010. It was one of the first technology offerings after the crisis, and the stock rose sharply on its first day. Assets under its management grew for years. In 2018 Hellman & Friedman bought the company for about $3 billion and merged it with Edelman Financial. The combined firm paired online advice for workplace savers with in-person planning for wealthier clients.

cover.theme: a model steam engine (a steady engine)

dek: QuinStreet found people shopping for a degree, a policy or a loan, and sold their interest to companies.
lede: Few consumers knew QuinStreet's name, but many had filled out one of its forms. It ran websites and campaigns that drew in people shopping for a degree, an insurance policy or a loan. Then it passed their interest to schools and companies, which paid per qualified lead or click. In early 2010 its biggest market was for-profit education. That industry was booming as unemployed adults went back to school.

sections.heading: Results Over Impressions
sections.body: Doug Valenti and Bronwyn Syiek founded QuinStreet in 1999. Their bet was that advertisers would rather pay for results than for impressions. A company could earn a margin by matching high-intent shoppers to buyers. QuinStreet built and bought content sites in its chosen fields. It invested in the data needed to price each lead. Advertisers paid only for results, and QuinStreet carried the risk of turning ad spending into qualified leads.

sections.heading: From Colleges to Insurance
sections.body: QuinStreet priced its IPO at $15 a share in February 2010. New federal rules on for-profit colleges soon cut into its largest business, and the stock fell. The company shifted toward insurance and financial services, where demand grew. Through all the changes, its model stayed much the same: advertisers still paid for results. QuinStreet remains publicly traded on the Nasdaq.

cover.artwork: Morning, Crossroads of the Forts de Marlotte

tagline: Census Rolls in the Living Room
dek: Ancestry let families trace their roots from home, using billions of scanned historical records.
lede: Ancestry.com scanned billions of census rolls, ship manifests and military files so people could hunt for their great-grandparents from the couch. Then it sold subscriptions to anyone building a family tree. It filed to go public in 2009, during a deep recession, and its subscriber count was still rising. Many subscribers stayed for years. They kept adding branches to their trees as new records came online.

sections.heading: A Utah Hobby Goes National
sections.body: The company's roots go back to a genealogy publisher in Utah, a state with a deep tradition of family history research. Its bet was that genealogy could become a mass market if the records were searchable from home. Ancestry spent years and large sums scanning and indexing records. Every page it added made the collection harder to copy. Rivals could not easily match it.

sections.heading: Spit in a Tube
sections.body: Ancestry priced its IPO at $13.50 a share in November 2009. In 2010 NBC began airing Who Do You Think You Are?, a show Ancestry sponsored. Subscribers kept growing. In 2012 the company launched AncestryDNA, which sold millions of saliva kits and linked customers to relatives they had never met. That same year a group led by Permira took Ancestry private for about $1.6 billion. Blackstone bought the company in 2020.

dek: Vitacost sold vitamins and supplements online for less than the health food store down the street.
lede: Vitacost made many of the supplements it sold, and that fattened its margins. It sold vitamins and health products online at low prices, alongside national brands. It shipped from its own warehouses to customers across the country. Shoppers liked the deep discounts and the brands their local stores did not carry. Vitacost went public in September 2009, when few retailers were growing and online shopping kept gaining ground.

sections.heading: A Catalog That Went Online
sections.body: Wayne Gorsek founded the business in 1994 as a catalog company. He bet that people who bought supplements regularly would shop by price and convenience. A direct seller, he reasoned, could beat the markup of health food stores. Vitacost moved online early and invested in its own manufacturing. Free shipping thresholds and frequent coupons kept customers reordering every few months.

sections.heading: Kroger Buys the Warehouses
sections.body: Vitacost priced its IPO at $12 a share in September 2009. Its years as a public company were hard, with management turnover, accounting questions and losses. In 2014 the grocery chain Kroger bought Vitacost for about $280 million to build up its online health business. Kroger kept Vitacost running as an online store. It used Vitacost's warehouses and know-how to ship health products to its own shoppers.

dek: OpenTable let diners book a restaurant table online in seconds, at any hour.
lede: Chuck Templeton's wife once spent about three and a half hours on the phone trying to book a dinner reservation. OpenTable was his answer. Diners could book a table online in seconds. Behind that simple service sat a computer system at the host stand of thousands of restaurants, managing seating and reservations. Restaurants paid a monthly fee for the system and a small charge for each diner the website sent.

sections.heading: Restaurant by Restaurant
sections.body: Templeton founded the company in 1998. The bet was that both sides needed help. Diners wanted to book at any hour, and restaurants wanted to fill seats and know their guests. OpenTable started in San Francisco and a handful of other big cities. It spent years installing its system one restaurant at a time, city by city. Only then did the network effects take hold.

sections.heading: A Bright Spot in 2009
sections.body: OpenTable priced its IPO at $20 a share in May 2009, in the depths of the recession. Restaurants were hurting, and few tech companies dared to list. The stock rose sharply on its first day. OpenTable expanded to more cities and to mobile booking. In 2014 Priceline, now Booking Holdings, bought OpenTable for about $2.6 billion, and OpenTable kept growing in cities around the world.

cover.artwork: Lunch at the Restaurant Fournaise (The Rowers' Lunch)

dek: SolarWinds sold IT administrators cheap, downloadable tools that warned them when their networks broke.
lede: SolarWinds sold enterprise software with no large sales force. It offered downloadable trials, low prices and a strong online community instead. Its tools were for the people who keep networks running. The software watched routers, servers and applications and warned administrators when something went wrong. SolarWinds filed to go public in 2009, one of the few tech listings of that bleak year.

sections.heading: Father and Son in Tulsa
sections.body: Donald Yonce and his son David started the company in Tulsa, Oklahoma, in 1999. Their bet was that IT staff would buy practical, affordable tools themselves, without long sales cycles. Prices were low enough that an administrator could often buy without asking a committee. The Yonces built a loyal following through free tools and online forums. The company later moved its headquarters to Austin.

sections.heading: Orion and the Hack
sections.body: SolarWinds priced its IPO at $12.50 a share in May 2009. Silver Lake and Thoma Bravo took it private in 2016, and it listed again in 2018. In 2020 hackers compromised its Orion software in one of the most serious cyberattacks in American history. Its products stayed a fixture in IT departments anyway. In 2025 Turn/River Capital took the company private for about $4.4 billion.

fate: Taken private by Apollo, 2016 ($4.3B); relisted 2020 (NASDAQ: RXT)
dek: Rackspace ran companies' servers for them and answered the phone, day or night, when something broke.
lede: Rackspace built its whole company around a promise it called Fanatical Support. Customers rented dedicated machines in Rackspace data centers. They paid extra for a team that managed those machines day and night and answered the phone when they broke. When Rackspace went public in August 2008, the financial system was weeks from collapse. Amazon's new cloud was also starting to change what hosting meant.

sections.heading: Three Students in San Antonio
sections.body: Three Trinity University students, Richard Yoo, Dirk Elmendorf and Pat Condon, started the company in San Antonio in 1998. Investor Graham Weston soon joined to lead it. Their bet was that most businesses did not want to run their own servers. Service would set a hosting company apart from its rivals. Rackspace grew quickly by serving small and midsize businesses that had no IT staff.

sections.heading: OpenStack, Apollo and Back
sections.body: Rackspace priced its IPO at $12.50 a share in August 2008 on the New York Stock Exchange. It launched a cloud business, and in 2010 it co-founded the OpenStack project with NASA. Competition from Amazon, Microsoft and Google squeezed it. Apollo took Rackspace private in 2016 for about $4.3 billion, and it returned to the public market in 2020. Today it mostly helps customers run workloads on the big public clouds.

tagline: Larry Ellison's Bet on the Cloud
dek: NetSuite let growing companies run their books, orders and inventory in a web browser.
lede: NetSuite went public under the one-letter ticker N, with Larry Ellison's money behind it. Its software handled a company's accounting, orders, inventory and customer records in one system, hosted on NetSuite's servers and sold by subscription. In 2007, enterprise software still mostly meant installing large packages on company computers. NetSuite was one of the first to show that a business's core financial system could live in the cloud.

sections.heading: An Oracle Veteran Leaves Home
sections.body: Evan Goldberg, a former Oracle executive, founded the company in 1998 with backing from Larry Ellison. The bet was that small and midsize businesses would trade the cost and hassle of installed software for one integrated online service. NetSuite spent years building its product while the market for cloud software slowly matured. Ellison's backing gave the young company money and credibility while it waited.

sections.heading: Back Home to Oracle
sections.body: NetSuite priced its IPO at $26 a share in December 2007 on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock fell hard in the 2008 crash. Then cloud software won acceptance, and growth returned. By 2016 NetSuite served thousands of midsize businesses. That year Oracle bought NetSuite for about $9.3 billion, and the deal made Oracle a major player in cloud software for running a business.

tagline: Public School at the Kitchen Table
dek: K12 let kids take a full public school course load from home, with certified teachers online.
lede: K12 ran public schools that students attended from their kitchen tables. It built an online curriculum and ran virtual charter schools for states and districts. Students took a full course load from a computer at home, with certified teachers on the other end. When K12 went public in December 2007, online learning was still unfamiliar to most parents. The idea of a public company running schools drew sharp debate.

sections.heading: A Banker and Bill Bennett
sections.body: Ron Packard, a former banker and McKinsey consultant, founded K12 in 2000 with backing from Knowledge Universe. Former Education Secretary William Bennett was its first chairman. The bet was that families wanted more choice in schooling, and that a strong online curriculum could serve students anywhere. K12 earned most of its revenue from public funds that followed students to its schools.

sections.heading: The Pandemic Enrollment Surge
sections.body: K12 priced its IPO at $18 a share in December 2007 on the New York Stock Exchange. Enrollment grew for years, and so did criticism of student results at some of its schools. In 2020 the company renamed itself Stride, and the pandemic sent enrollment sharply higher. Its business now spans online public schools, private online schools and career training. It still trades under its original ticker, LRN.

tagline: Hundreds of Hobby Sites, One Company
dek: Internet Brands ran hundreds of small websites and forums, each built for one loyal crowd.
lede: Internet Brands started as a website for buying a car and ended up owning WebMD. In between, it bought and built hundreds of focused sites and communities on cars, home improvement, travel, health and law. Each one was small. Together they drew a large audience and steady advertising. The company began as CarsDirect, and it went public in November 2007, just before the financial crisis.

sections.heading: When CarsDirect Changed Course
sections.body: CarsDirect was started at Bill Gross's Idealab in 1998, with Scott Painter. It was one of the early bets that people would buy big-ticket items online. When that market proved hard, the company changed course. It began buying established enthusiast sites and forums cheaply. Then it ran them on shared technology and sold advertising across the network. Each site already had a loyal, specific audience.

sections.heading: The Buyer of WebMD
sections.body: Internet Brands priced its IPO at $8 a share in November 2007 on the Nasdaq, below its planned range of $10 to $12. In 2010 Hellman & Friedman bought the company for about $640 million. KKR later acquired it. The company kept growing by buying communities and specialist sites. In 2017 Internet Brands bought WebMD, another company in this directory, and became a major force in online health.

cover.theme: a shop front (a network of niche sites)

dek: American Public Education let soldiers and veterans earn a degree online from wherever they were posted.
lede: American Public Education kept its prices close to the military's tuition assistance cap, which made it an easy choice for people in uniform. Its American Military University and American Public University offered degrees that soldiers, sailors and veterans could finish from anywhere. When it filed in 2007, for-profit online colleges were growing fast. APEI stood out for its low tuition and its military focus.

sections.heading: A Marine's Mobile Campus
sections.body: James Etter, a retired Marine officer, founded American Military University in 1991. His bet was simple. Service members move often and deploy far from campus, so they needed a university that went with them. The school kept its admissions open and taught online. Military tuition assistance often paid for the degrees. Courses started every month, which suited students on shifting military schedules.

sections.heading: Nursing and Civilians
sections.body: APEI priced its IPO at $20 a share in November 2007 on the Nasdaq, and the stock climbed in its early years. Enrollment later slowed as for-profit education faced tighter federal rules. The company expanded into nursing education through acquisitions. The American Public University System remains its core, and it now serves many civilian students alongside service members. APEI remains publicly traded on the Nasdaq.

dek: SoundBite let banks and utilities send reminder calls, texts and emails without owning any call center equipment.
lede: When a bank, utility or collection agency called to remind someone about a payment, the call often came from SoundBite. Its hosted system placed reminder calls, payment notices and alerts by voice, text and email. Clients needed no equipment of their own, because SoundBite sold the service over the internet. It filed to go public in 2007, when hosted software was still a new way to sell.

sections.heading: Collections First
sections.body: SoundBite started in 2000 with a bet that outbound customer contact could move from call center hardware to a hosted service. Its first big market was collections. There, reaching more people at the right time had a direct value. It later added more channels and pitched friendlier uses, such as appointment reminders and fraud alerts. Clients paid by usage, so revenue rose with each campaign they ran.

sections.heading: Into Genesys
sections.body: SoundBite priced its IPO at $8 a share in November 2007, weeks before the financial crisis began to bite. Its stock stayed low for most of its life as a public company. In 2013 Genesys, the contact center software maker, bought SoundBite for about $100 million. Genesys folded SoundBite's outbound tools into its larger platform. Clients could then handle calls in both directions in one place.

cover.theme: a bell being rung (a call to customers)

dek: Maxcom gave Mexican homes and small businesses an alternative to Telmex for phone, internet and TV.
lede: Maxcom picked a fight with Telmex, the company that had long dominated Mexican telecom. It sold local phone service, internet and later pay television to homes and small businesses in Mexico City, Puebla and other cities. It built its own lines and fiber to do it. Maxcom listed its shares on the New York Stock Exchange in 2007. Emerging markets were in favor, and investors were hunting for growth in Latin America.

sections.heading: When Mexico Opened the Lines
sections.body: Maxcom was founded in 1996, after Mexico opened local telephone service to competition. The bet was that a nimble new carrier could win customers from a slow incumbent. It would build modern networks in selected cities and bundle its services. Maxcom invested heavily in its own lines and fiber. Like many challengers, it faced the hard economics of building physical networks street by street.

sections.heading: Debt, Then Delisting
sections.body: Maxcom priced its New York listing at $17.50 per American depositary share in October 2007. The financial crisis and fierce competition hurt the business. The company went through debt troubles and a restructuring. In 2014 it delisted from the New York Stock Exchange, and its board cited low trading volume in the United States. Its shares kept trading in Mexico, and over the counter in the United States.

dek: Constant Contact let a florist, a dentist or a church send a good-looking email newsletter without hiring help.
lede: Constant Contact taught small businesses to send email newsletters, and it did much of the teaching in person. Its online service gave a florist, a dentist or a church easy templates, a home for a mailing list and reports on who opened each message. The company backed this with seminars and phone coaching across the country. By 2007 it had tens of thousands of customers paying monthly. Most were tiny organizations.

sections.heading: Roving Software Finds Email
sections.body: Randy Parker founded the company in 1995 as Roving Software. The bet was that small organizations wanted to keep in touch with their customers but lacked the skills of big marketers. Gail Goodman became chief executive in 1999 and focused the company on email marketing. She built its sales engine around free trials and radio ads. Customer service and education became central to how it sold.

sections.heading: Endurance, Then Independence
sections.body: Constant Contact priced its IPO at $16 a share in October 2007 on the Nasdaq. It added tools for social media and events, and it kept growing through the downturn. In 2016 Endurance International Group bought the company for about $1.1 billion. Endurance kept Constant Contact as a separate brand. Later, under private equity owners, Constant Contact became a separate company again.

cover.artwork: Messenger with a Letter, from the series "Elegant Five-needled Pine (Furyu goyo no matsu)"

tagline: The Deal That Kept eBay Out
dek: MercadoLibre let people across Latin America buy and sell online and trust strangers with their money.
lede: eBay bought a stake in MercadoLibre and agreed to stay out of Latin America, leaving the region to a startup from Buenos Aires. MercadoLibre let people in Argentina, Brazil, Mexico and other countries buy and sell new and used goods online. Its payment service, MercadoPago, let them trust strangers with their money. When it went public in August 2007, it was one of the few Latin American internet companies to list in New York.

sections.heading: A Stanford Business Plan
sections.body: Marcos Galperin started MercadoLibre in 1999 while studying at Stanford Business School. He launched it in Buenos Aires with Hernán Kazah. The bet was that e-commerce in Latin America needed a local champion that understood its markets, currencies and logistics. eBay's stake came two years later, in 2001, along with its promise to stay out of the region. The company later moved its base to Montevideo, Uruguay.

sections.heading: Bigger Than the Marketplace
sections.body: MercadoLibre priced its IPO at $18 a share in August 2007 on the Nasdaq. It built its own shipping network and turned MercadoPago into a major fintech business. That arm now offers digital wallets, loans and payments to people across the region, far beyond the marketplace. MercadoLibre became one of the most valuable companies in Latin America, and it remains publicly traded on the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: the road to market (a great marketplace)

tagline: A Background Check in One Click
dek: HireRight let big employers check a job candidate's record with a click instead of a stack of paperwork.
lede: Many Fortune 500 companies ran their new hires past HireRight before the first day of work. Employers ordered criminal, education, employment and drug screens through its website. HireRight then gathered the results from courts and records across the country and abroad. Most of its clients were large companies that hired in volume. When it filed in 2007, background screening had become standard practice in American hiring.

sections.heading: Plugged Into the Hiring System
sections.body: HireRight was founded in 1995. Its bet was that the slow, paper-based business of employment screening could move onto the internet. It built software that plugged into employers' hiring systems. A check could start with a click, and the results could flow straight back. That integration won it large corporate accounts. International checks became a strength as global companies screened candidates in many countries.

sections.heading: A Year on the Nasdaq
sections.body: HireRight priced its IPO at $15 a share in August 2007 on the Nasdaq. Its time as a public company was short. In 2008 US Investigations Services, a large provider of government background checks, bought HireRight for $19.75 a share in cash. The HireRight name lived on. It later returned to the public market as a separate company, then was taken private again.

cover.artwork: Ornament with Owl Mocked by Day Birds

dek: Monotype licensed the fonts that printers, phones, cars and software used to put words on screens and pages.
lede: Monotype began with a machine that cast metal type one letter at a time. By 2007 it owned many of the letters the world reads, including Helvetica and Times New Roman. It licensed fonts and font technology to the makers of printers, phones, cars and software. Most people never saw its name. Its type appeared on billions of screens and pages, and its fonts were built into many office laser printers.

sections.heading: From Hot Metal to Pixels
sections.body: Tolbert Lanston invented the Monotype machine in the 1880s. The company survived the move from hot metal to photo type to digital fonts by holding on to its library and its craft. Its modern bet was that fonts were intellectual property. Device makers would license them, one unit at a time. In 2006 it bought Linotype, the German type house whose library included Helvetica.

sections.heading: Fonts for Brands
sections.body: Monotype Imaging priced its IPO at $12 a share in July 2007 on the Nasdaq. It bought more type libraries, including Ascender in 2010. It built a large business licensing fonts to brands and developers, and sold them through its Fonts.com site. In 2019 the private equity firm HGGC took Monotype private for about $825 million. Its fonts are still licensed to device makers, software companies and global brands.

cover.theme: a printer at work (type and printing)

dek: Orbitz let travelers compare fares and book flights, hotels and packages in one fast search.
lede: Orbitz started as a project of five big American airlines that wanted their own answer to Expedia and Travelocity. The site sold flights, hotels and vacation packages online. By 2007 Orbitz Worldwide also included ebookers in Europe and HotelClub in Asia Pacific. It was one of the largest online travel companies in the world, and a generation of travelers knew its name.

sections.heading: Five Airlines, One Website
sections.body: The airlines formed the company in 1999 and launched the site in 2001. Their bet was that, together, they could sell their own tickets online more cheaply than through outside agents. Orbitz won customers with a fast search engine and a clear display of fares. Cendant bought Orbitz in 2004. In 2006 Blackstone bought Cendant's travel arm, Travelport, which later spun Orbitz Worldwide out to the public.

sections.heading: Bought by Its Old Rival
sections.body: Orbitz Worldwide priced its IPO at $15 a share in July 2007 on the New York Stock Exchange. The recession and heavy debt soon pressed on the business, and the stock fell far below its offering price. In 2015 Expedia bought Orbitz for about $1.6 billion. The airlines' answer to Expedia now belonged to Expedia. Orbitz kept running as a separate brand there, alongside Travelocity and CheapTickets.

fate: Still public as DHI Group (NYSE: DHX)
dek: Dice let tech workers find their next job, and let employers search for the résumés they needed.
lede: Dice started as an electronic bulletin board for computer contractors, years before the web. By 2007 it was where technology workers looked for jobs. Its board listed openings for programmers, engineers and IT staff. Employers paid to post jobs and search its database of résumés, and job seekers used the site free. Dice Holdings also owned boards for finance and energy professionals. It filed to go public as tech hiring was brisk.

sections.heading: A Narrow, Valuable Crowd
sections.body: Dice began in 1990, when its users dialed in to a bulletin board instead of browsing a website. The bet was that specialists wanted a job board built for their field. Programmers, engineers and IT staff came to Dice to look for work, and recruiters followed them there. That audience was hard to reach any other way. So Dice could charge employers more for job postings and résumé searches.

sections.heading: LinkedIn Arrives
sections.body: Dice Holdings priced its IPO at $13 a share in July 2007 on the New York Stock Exchange. Its business rose and fell with tech hiring. LinkedIn became a strong rival for recruiters' budgets. The company renamed itself DHI Group. It later sold its finance and energy boards and returned its focus to technology careers. DHI Group remains publicly traded on the New York Stock Exchange.

dek: Comscore told websites and advertisers how many people visited, and what those people did online.
lede: Comscore recruited a large panel of internet users who agreed to let it track their browsing. It sold the resulting data to websites, advertisers and investors. Its monthly rankings of the most visited sites became a standard reference, and its data fed investor research on internet companies. In 2007 online advertising was growing fast. Buyers wanted numbers they could trust.

sections.heading: Watching the Panel Shop
sections.body: Gian Fulgoni and Magid Abraham, veterans of the market research firm Information Resources, founded Comscore in 1999. Their bet was that the internet needed a ratings system like television had, built on much richer data about behavior. They built the panel first and then sold subscriptions to the reports. The panel showed Comscore more than traffic. It saw what people bought and searched for.

sections.heading: Delisted, Then Back
sections.body: Comscore priced its IPO at $16.50 a share in June 2007 on the Nasdaq. In 2016 it merged with Rentrak to measure television too. Accounting problems led to its delisting in 2018 and a restatement. It later returned to the Nasdaq, where it still trades. Its business now centers on measuring audiences across television, streaming and digital media, for advertisers and the media companies that sell to them.

dek: Limelight delivered video streams, downloads and web pages fast to people anywhere in the world.
lede: Akamai sued Limelight Networks for patent infringement a year before Limelight went public. The two were fighting over the same ground. Limelight ran a global network of servers that moved the internet's heaviest files: video streams, software downloads and web pages. Its customers ranged from video sites to software and game companies. In 2007 online video was exploding, and Limelight was the main challenger to Akamai, the leader in content delivery.

sections.heading: Built for Big Files
sections.body: Limelight was founded in Arizona in 2001. Its bet was that a new network, built with large data centers and its own fiber links, could deliver rich media more cheaply than older designs. It focused on video and large files, where speed and capacity mattered most. The company won big video customers early and grew quickly alongside them. A few large customers made up much of its revenue.

sections.heading: Edgecast, Edgio, Bankruptcy
sections.body: Limelight priced its IPO at $15 a share in June 2007 on the Nasdaq, as online video took off. Akamai's lawsuit, filed in 2006, dragged on for years. Pricing pressure kept profits thin, and Limelight never matched the scale or profits of its larger rival. In 2022 Limelight bought Yahoo's Edgecast and renamed itself Edgio. Edgio filed for bankruptcy in 2024.

cover.theme: a singer on the stage (the limelight)
cover.artwork: On the Stage, plate one from Yvette Guilbert

fate: Merged with Informa Tech, 2024; still public (NASDAQ: TTGT)
dek: TechTarget gave IT buyers free research, and told tech vendors who was reading it.
lede: TechTarget gave away white papers and research, then told technology vendors who had downloaded them. Its many sites covered storage, security, networking and other topics in depth for people who buy technology at work. Readers registered to download. Vendors paid TechTarget to reach those readers and to receive leads on who was researching a purchase. In 2007 trade magazines were losing ground, and TechTarget's online model was taking their place.

sections.heading: Catching Buyers Mid-Search
sections.body: Greg Strakosch and Don Hawk founded TechTarget in 1999. Their bet was that specialized content could attract IT professionals at the moment they were researching purchases. Vendors would pay well to know who those readers were. The company built dozens of focused sites, each aimed at a narrow group of buyers. Readers got free content, and vendors paid to reach them.

sections.heading: Informa Takes Control
sections.body: TechTarget priced its IPO at $13 a share in May 2007 on the Nasdaq. Over time it shifted further toward selling data on buying intent. In 2024 it combined with Informa Tech's digital businesses. The new company, majority owned by Informa, kept the TechTarget name and listing. Its sites still serve IT buyers, and its data on who is researching what remains its main product.

dek: Veraz Networks sold phone carriers the gear to carry voice calls over the internet for less.
lede: Veraz Networks sold gear that squeezed voice calls into less bandwidth, and carriers in emerging markets prized it. Its switches, media gateways and voice compression products let phone companies carry calls over internet networks, cutting costs and adding services. Most of its customers were carriers outside the United States. In 2007 carriers worldwide were in the middle of this long shift. Few consumers knew the Veraz name.

sections.heading: Saving Scarce Bandwidth
sections.body: Veraz bet that telephone carriers would replace their old circuit switches with software-based equipment for internet calling. It paired that switching gear with voice compression technology, which fit more calls into the same lines. Carriers in emerging markets valued it because bandwidth there was costly. The company had close ties to ECI Telecom, which owned a large stake. Its main rivals were much larger equipment makers.

sections.heading: Merged Into Dialogic
sections.body: Veraz priced its IPO at $8 a share in April 2007 on the Nasdaq, below its planned range of $10 to $12. ECI sold part of its stake in the offering. Competition from larger equipment makers and the 2008 downturn hurt sales. In 2010 Veraz merged with Dialogic, a communications technology company. The deal was in effect a reverse acquisition: Dialogic's owners held most of the combined company, which took the Dialogic name.

cover.theme: a field telegraph wagon (the voice network)

dek: Aruba let hospitals, universities and offices run thousands of secure Wi-Fi connections from one place.
lede: Aruba Networks went public months before the first iPhone, just as companies were deciding that wireless would be how people connected at work. Its access points and central controllers let a university, hospital or corporate campus run thousands of wireless connections securely from one place. Laptops had already made Wi-Fi a must. Hospitals, schools and offices were among its early customers.

sections.heading: Brains in the Controller
sections.body: Keerti Melkote and Pankaj Manglik founded Aruba in 2002. Their bet was that enterprise Wi-Fi needed central management and security. Scattered standalone access points would not do. Aruba put the intelligence in a central controller, which made large networks easier to secure and manage. It competed directly with Cisco, which dominated networking. It won customers that needed large, mobile and secure wireless networks.

sections.heading: HP Keeps the Name
sections.body: Aruba priced its IPO at $11 a share in March 2007 on the Nasdaq. Smartphones and tablets soon flooded offices and campuses, and demand for its gear grew. By 2015 Aruba had become a leading rival to Cisco in enterprise wireless. That year Hewlett-Packard bought Aruba for about $3 billion. The Aruba name lived on as HP's networking brand, and it remains at the center of HP's networking business.

dek: U.S. Auto Parts sold replacement car parts online for well below what dealers and repair shops charged.
lede: U.S. Auto Parts bought many of its bumpers, headlights and mirrors directly from manufacturers in Asia, then sold them online for well below dealer prices. Its websites and eBay listings covered parts for thousands of makes and models, from mirrors to engine parts. It shipped from its own warehouses. The company went public in early 2007, as do-it-yourself buyers were moving online.

sections.heading: Matching Part to Car
sections.body: The company started in 1995 selling auto parts, and it moved its business onto the internet. The bet was that car owners and small repair shops would buy parts online if the catalog was deep and the price was right. The hard part was matching the right part to the right vehicle. U.S. Auto Parts built its own catalog data to solve it.

sections.heading: Renamed CarParts.com
sections.body: U.S. Auto Parts priced its IPO at $10 a share in February 2007 on the Nasdaq. In the years that followed, search engine changes and competition hurt its traffic. The stock spent long stretches at low levels. The company later invested in new distribution centers to ship parts faster across the country. In 2020 it renamed itself CarParts.com, and it remains publicly traded.

cover.theme: a motor car in the street (car parts)

dek: Capella let working adults earn master's and doctoral degrees online, on their own schedule.
lede: Capella University was founded by a former chief executive of the toy company Tonka, and it taught working adults entirely online. Most students were mid-career and pursuing master's and doctoral degrees in business, education, psychology and nursing. Capella was regionally accredited, which mattered to employers and students alike. When it went public in November 2006, online higher education was growing fast and drawing new investor interest.

sections.heading: The Graduate School of America
sections.body: Stephen Shank founded Capella in 1991 as The Graduate School of America. The bet was that adults with jobs and families would pursue advanced degrees if they could study on their own schedule. Capella built its programs online from the start instead of adapting a campus model. It later added competency-based programs that let students move at their own pace.

sections.heading: Merged With Strayer
sections.body: Capella priced its IPO at $20 a share in November 2006 on the Nasdaq. Enrollment grew for several years, then slowed under tighter federal rules for for-profit schools. In 2018 Capella merged with Strayer Education, and the combined company became Strategic Education. Capella University still operates alongside Strayer University. It remains one of the largest online universities in the country, with students from every state and many countries.

cover.theme: the fates among the stars (Capella, a bright star)
cover.artwork: The Fates Gathering in the Stars

dek: Acme Packet made the boxes that let internet phone calls pass safely between carriers' networks.
lede: Every time an internet phone call crossed from one network into another, it needed a guard at the border. Acme Packet made those guards. Its session border controllers sat at the edges of carrier and enterprise networks. They connected voice and video calls, enforced security and kept quality high. In 2006 telephone companies were moving their networks onto internet technology. Its main customers were telephone carriers and cable operators.

sections.heading: Built for One Job
sections.body: Andy Ory and Patrick MeLampy had worked together at earlier networking companies. They founded Acme Packet in 2000. Their bet was that internet calling would need a dedicated device at each network border, and that carriers would pay for one built for the job. Early relationships with major carriers set up rapid growth. Acme Packet became the leader in a category it had defined.

sections.heading: Oracle's Communications Base
sections.body: Acme Packet priced its IPO at $9.50 a share in October 2006 on the Nasdaq. It was profitable and grew quickly as carriers and large businesses adopted internet calling. In 2013 Oracle bought Acme Packet for about $2.1 billion. Oracle made the business the base of its communications unit, selling the same products to carriers and large enterprises. Those products remain in use in many carrier networks.

dek: eHealth let people who bought their own health insurance compare plans and prices online.
lede: People who bought their own health insurance had few easy ways to compare plans until eHealth put them side by side. Its site, eHealthInsurance.com, showed plans from many insurers, so individuals, families and small businesses could weigh prices and coverage before buying. Insurers paid eHealth commissions on each sale. When it went public in 2006, most Americans still got their insurance through work.

sections.heading: A Broker in Every State
sections.body: eHealth started in 1997 with a bet that buying health insurance, a confusing and paper-heavy process, could work like other online shopping. It became a licensed broker in every state and built tools to quote and apply for plans online. Most of its customers bought insurance for themselves, such as the self-employed. Insurers paid it commissions for each policy, the same way they paid traditional agents.

sections.heading: The Medicare Turn
sections.body: eHealth priced its IPO at $14 a share in October 2006 on the Nasdaq. The Affordable Care Act and its public exchanges later changed the individual market. eHealth turned toward Medicare plans for older Americans. That business grew quickly as baby boomers aged into the program, and it became most of eHealth's revenue. Rising marketing costs and changing commissions made profits uneven. eHealth remains publicly traded.

cover.theme: lovers under an umbrella (coverage and protection)
cover.artwork: Lovers Beneath an Umbrella in the Snow

tagline: Photo Books From the Hard Drive
dek: Shutterfly turned the digital photos piling up on people's computers into prints, books and holiday cards.
lede: Shutterfly's busiest weeks came each December, when holiday cards and photo gifts drove a large share of the year's sales. As cameras went digital, people stopped printing film, and their pictures piled up on hard drives. Shutterfly let them upload photos, store them free and order prints, photo books, cards and calendars, made in its own plants. By 2006 photo books and holiday cards were its fastest-growing products.

sections.heading: Backed by Jim Clark
sections.body: Shutterfly was founded in 1999 with backing from Netscape co-founder Jim Clark, and Eva Manolis was among its founders. The bet was that digital photography would create a large market for high-quality printed products. Shutterfly ran its own manufacturing to control quality. Free unlimited photo storage was part of its offer from early on, and it kept customers coming back to order.

sections.heading: Tiny Prints and Lifetouch
sections.body: Shutterfly priced its IPO at $15 a share in September 2006 on the Nasdaq, with photo books and holiday cards leading its growth. Its customers were mostly families saving their memories. The company grew by buying other businesses, including Tiny Prints and, later, the school photo company Lifetouch. Its holiday season became a major retail event. In 2019 Apollo took Shutterfly private for about $2.7 billion.

dek: CommVault let big organizations back up, archive and recover all their data from one system.
lede: CommVault's software kept one index of everything a company had saved, while many rivals sold a separate tool for each job. It backed up, archived and recovered data across servers and storage systems, all from one platform. Its customers included many large enterprises and public agencies. In 2006 corporate data was growing fast, and new rules required businesses to keep their records and find them on demand.

sections.heading: Out of Bell Labs
sections.body: CommVault grew out of a data management group at Bell Labs and became an independent company in 1996. Its bet was that companies would want one integrated system for every kind of data protection instead of a patchwork. It sold mainly through partners such as Dell and storage resellers. Its single code base set it apart from rivals that stitched together products from acquisitions.

sections.heading: From Backup to Ransomware
sections.body: CommVault priced its IPO at $14.50 a share in September 2006 on the Nasdaq. It grew into one of the leading backup software companies. Many customers first bought it for basic backup, then used it for archiving and compliance. Later CommVault moved its products to the cloud and added protection against ransomware. It serves large enterprises and government agencies around the world, and it remains publicly traded on the Nasdaq.

cover.artwork: The Giant Wheel, plate 9 from Imaginary Prisons

dek: Riverbed made files and applications open quickly in branch offices far from the company's data center.
lede: Riverbed made far-away offices feel close. Its Steelhead appliances sat at each end of a company's wide area network and cut the data crossing it. Files and applications opened quickly in branch offices. In 2006 companies were pulling servers back into central data centers to save money. Slow links to remote offices had become a daily complaint, and Riverbed's customers ranged from law firms to global manufacturers.

sections.heading: Smarter Software Over Bandwidth
sections.body: Jerry Kennelly and Steve McCanne founded Riverbed in 2002. McCanne was a computer scientist known for research on internet video. Their bet was that smarter software could fix slow networks without more bandwidth. Riverbed combined data deduplication and protocol tricks in a box that was easy to install. Customers often saw results in days, which made the boxes an easy sale, and revenue grew quickly.

sections.heading: Thoma Bravo and a Restructuring
sections.body: Riverbed priced its IPO at $9.75 a share in September 2006 on the Nasdaq and soon traded well above it. It led the WAN optimization market for years. As applications moved to the cloud, growth slowed. In 2015 Thoma Bravo took Riverbed private for about $3.6 billion. It went through a debt restructuring in 2021, and it still sells network performance tools.

dek: Omniture showed online stores where their visitors came from, what they did and what they bought.
lede: Omniture watched every page view and click on many of the largest retail websites in the country. Its SiteCatalyst service showed marketers where visitors came from, what they did and what they bought. Large retailers and media companies paid for it by subscription. In 2006 online sales were booming. Measuring them had become a job for serious software, and Omniture was ready to go public.

sections.heading: Two Founders in Utah
sections.body: Josh James and John Pestana, two young Utah entrepreneurs, founded the company in 1996. Their bet was that businesses would want detailed, real-time data on their online customers. They would pay for it as a hosted service. Omniture won large clients and later added tools for testing and targeting. Customers paid by volume, so Omniture's revenue grew as their websites grew.

sections.heading: Now Adobe Analytics
sections.body: Omniture priced its IPO at $6.50 a share in June 2006 on the Nasdaq. It grew quickly and bought rivals. The biggest was Visual Sciences, the company once called WebSideStory, in a deal worth about $394 million that closed in early 2008. In 2009 Adobe bought Omniture for about $1.8 billion. Its software became the core of Adobe's marketing business and lives on today as Adobe Analytics.

cover.artwork: The Eye, Like a Strange Balloon Moves Towards Infinity, plate one from To Edgar Poe

dek: LoopNet let brokers, buyers and tenants find offices, shops and warehouses for sale or lease online.
lede: LoopNet let commercial brokers list properties for free, and that is how it became the largest marketplace of its kind in the United States. Brokers posted offices, shops, warehouses and apartment buildings for sale or lease. Buyers and tenants searched them free or with premium memberships. LoopNet also sold data on property sales and comparables. When it went public in 2006, commercial real estate was booming.

sections.heading: Out of the Flyer Business
sections.body: Dennis DeAndre started LoopNet in San Francisco in 1995. The bet was that commercial real estate, a business of private networks and printed flyers, would move its listings online. Free listings drew brokers in fast. LoopNet then charged its heaviest users, the people who listed and searched the most, for premium features. That model built a base of listings that rivals could not match.

sections.heading: CoStar Wins Approval
sections.body: LoopNet priced its IPO at $12 a share in June 2006 on the Nasdaq. It stayed profitable through the property downturn of 2008 and 2009. In 2012 CoStar, the commercial property data company, bought LoopNet for about $860 million after regulators approved the deal. LoopNet still runs as a CoStar brand. Its listings remain a standard stop for anyone searching for commercial property.

dek: Vonage let people keep their phone number and call anywhere in the country for one flat monthly fee.
lede: Vonage offered some of its own customers shares in its IPO, and the stock fell on its first day. Those customers were angry. They had signed up for a simple idea. They plugged a small adapter into their broadband connection, kept a regular phone number and got unlimited calling across the country for a flat monthly fee. Vonage's ads were everywhere. By 2006 it had more than a million and a half subscribers.

sections.heading: A Trader's Phone Company
sections.body: Jeffrey Citron, a former electronic trading entrepreneur, started Vonage in 2001. The bet was that broadband homes would drop expensive landline plans for internet calling if it felt like a normal phone. Its flat monthly fee for unlimited calls undercut traditional phone plans by a wide margin. Vonage spent heavily on marketing to win customers fast, and it lost a lot of money doing so.

sections.heading: From Homes to Business
sections.body: Vonage priced its IPO at $17 a share in May 2006 on the New York Stock Exchange. It was the best-known challenger to the old phone companies. The stock kept falling after its first day. Patent suits from Verizon added to its trouble, and the cable companies were coming for the same customers. Vonage later rebuilt itself around business communications. In 2022 Ericsson bought it for about $6.2 billion.

dek: Liquidity Services sold surplus and returned goods online, from retailers' extra stock to government vehicles.
lede: Liquidity Services won its biggest early contract by selling off U.S. military surplus. It ran online auctions for goods others no longer needed, from excess inventory at big retailers to used vehicles and equipment from government agencies. Much of that surplus had gone to slow local auctions or to scrap. Buyers ranged from small resellers to large exporters. When it filed in 2006, Liquidity Services was turning a dusty corner of commerce into a steady online business.

sections.heading: Better Prices Than Scrap
sections.body: William Angrick founded the company in 1999. The bet was that surplus goods would fetch better prices online, in front of many more buyers. Liquidity Services won large contracts with the Defense Department. It built sites such as Liquidation.com and GovDeals, where buyers bid against each other. Its sellers paid a share of each sale, so the company earned more as prices rose.

sections.heading: When the Contracts Shrank
sections.body: Liquidity Services priced its IPO at $10 a share in February 2006 on the Nasdaq. It grew for years on its military surplus contracts. Then it lost some of them, and the stock swung widely. The company refocused on retail returns and government surplus. Its marketplaces still handle large volumes of goods from public agencies and retailers, and it remains publicly traded on the Nasdaq.

cover.theme: the clothes exchange after the sale (surplus)
cover.artwork: After the Sale, Clothes Exchange, Houndsditch

dek: NightHawk let small radiology groups sleep through the night while doctors abroad read their emergency scans.
lede: NightHawk Radiology read America's overnight X-rays and CT scans from Sydney and Zurich, where it was daytime. Hospitals sent their emergency images over the internet to U.S.-trained, U.S.-licensed radiologists working there. Reports came back in minutes. In 2006 emergency rooms were scanning more patients than ever. Small radiology groups struggled to cover every night, and NightHawk covered those nights for them.

sections.heading: An Idaho Radiologist's Idea
sections.body: Paul Berger, a radiologist in Idaho, co-founded NightHawk in 2001. The bet was that time zones could solve the overnight staffing problem. Radiology groups would gladly pay to give their doctors a full night's sleep. The hard part was paperwork. NightHawk handled licensing and credentials across many states, so each of its radiologists held licenses in many states at once.

sections.heading: Merged Into vRad
sections.body: NightHawk priced its IPO at $16 a share in February 2006 on the Nasdaq. Competition and pricing pressure grew, and many radiology groups began to cover nights themselves. In 2010 Virtual Radiologic bought NightHawk for about $170 million. The combined company, under the vRad name, became the largest teleradiology provider in the United States. Its overnight model is now standard practice in American hospitals.

dek: Traffic.com told drivers where the jams were, live, on the radio, the web and the car's navigation screen.
lede: Traffic.com installed its own sensors along major roads in dozens of American cities to find out where the jams were. It combined that data with other sources and sent live traffic reports to radio and TV stations, websites, phones and in-car navigation. Its reports reached millions of listeners each day. In early 2006 GPS devices were spreading fast. Live traffic was the feature drivers wanted next.

sections.heading: One Dataset, Many Buyers
sections.body: Traffic.com began in 1998 with a bet that accurate, real-time traffic data would be valuable to many outlets at once. Its own sensor network gave it data rivals did not have. It earned money from licensing that data. It also sold advertising in the traffic reports it produced for broadcasters. Selling the same data many times over was the core of its plan.

sections.heading: Into Navteq's Maps
sections.body: Traffic.com priced its IPO at $12 a share in January 2006 on the Nasdaq. The company struggled to turn its costly sensor network into a profit. Within a year Navteq, the digital map maker, agreed to buy it. The deal closed in 2007 at about $179 million. Navteq, later bought by Nokia, folded the traffic data into the maps used by car navigation systems.

dek: DealerTrack let car dealers send a buyer's credit application to many lenders at once and hear back in minutes.
lede: Before DealerTrack, a car dealer faxed a buyer's credit application to lenders one at a time and waited. DealerTrack's network let the dealer send it to many lenders at once and get answers back in minutes. By 2005 a large share of American franchised dealers used it. DealerTrack was now selling more software to run the rest of the dealership.

sections.heading: Backed by the Lenders
sections.body: DealerTrack was formed in 2001 with backing from several large auto lenders. The bet was that a neutral online network for credit applications would speed up car sales for everyone. Lenders paid a fee for each application. Dealers signed on because the system was simple and saved time on the showroom floor. Every new lender made the network more useful to dealers, so scale became an advantage.

sections.heading: Joining Autotrader and Kelley
sections.body: DealerTrack priced its IPO at $17 a share in December 2005 on the Nasdaq, as it pushed beyond credit applications. It grew through many acquisitions, adding dealer management systems, compliance tools and Dealer.com. In 2015 Cox Automotive bought DealerTrack for about $4 billion. Cox combined it with brands such as Autotrader and Kelley Blue Book, building one of the largest companies in automotive software.

dek: Vocus gave public relations teams one place online to find reporters, send releases and track coverage.
lede: Public relations work still ran largely on phone calls and spreadsheets when Vocus moved it into a web browser. Its online service kept databases of journalists and outlets, sent press releases, tracked news coverage and measured results. Corporations, agencies and government offices paid for it by subscription, which made its revenue steady and predictable. Vocus filed to go public in 2005, as the move to online tools was just starting.

sections.heading: Rolodex to Database
sections.body: Rick Rudman and Bob Lentz founded the company in 1992. They bet that public relations, a craft run on personal contacts and phone calls, would adopt software for its daily work. Vocus moved early to a hosted model and sold it by subscription. Later it bought PRWeb, the online press release service. Its customers ranged from small agencies to large corporations and government offices.

sections.heading: Folded Into Cision
sections.body: Vocus priced its IPO at $9 a share in December 2005 on the Nasdaq. It grew steadily and added marketing tools for small businesses, with mixed results. In 2014 the private equity firm GTCR took Vocus private for about $446 million and combined it with Cision. The combined company kept the Cision name. It became one of the largest providers of public relations software in the world.

dek: WebMD explained conditions, drugs and treatments in plain language to anyone who searched their symptoms.
lede: When WebMD Health went public in 2005, it was a unit of Emdeon, the company once called Healtheon/WebMD, and the offering sold only a minority stake. By then its site was where Americans went to look up their symptoms. It explained conditions, drugs and treatments in plain language. Its sister site, Medscape, served doctors. Drug makers and health companies paid to advertise to both audiences.

sections.heading: What Survived the Dot-Com Dream
sections.body: WebMD came out of the dot-com era. Jeff Arnold founded it in 1998, and it soon merged with Jim Clark's Healtheon. The early dream was to wire the whole health care system. What lasted was simpler: a trusted source of health information for consumers, paid for by advertising and sponsorships. The consumer site and Medscape together gave it reach to both patients and doctors.

sections.heading: The Internet Brands Deal
sections.body: WebMD Health priced its IPO at $17.50 a share in September 2005 on the Nasdaq. It later became fully independent of its parent and stayed the top health site for years. In 2017 Internet Brands, another company in this directory and by then owned by KKR, bought WebMD for about $2.8 billion. The site remains one of the most visited health information sources in the United States.

tagline: The Back Office of Business Travel
dek: TRX handled the routine work behind business trips, so travel agencies and corporations did not have to.
lede: TRX tried to go public in 2001, pulled the deal when markets turned, and finally listed in 2005. It worked behind the scenes of business travel. TRX processed bookings and transactions for travel agencies and corporate travel managers, and it ran reservation and customer support services. Its data tools showed companies how their employees traveled. By 2005 online booking was spreading, and travel agencies were outsourcing more of their back-office work.

sections.heading: Call Centers and Data
sections.body: TRX bet that travel agencies and corporations would hand off the routine, high-volume work of processing travel to a specialist. It combined hosted technology with call centers and processing staff. Over time it put more weight on travel data. Its corporate data business showed companies where their travel money went and where they could save. That data also gave them leverage to negotiate with airlines and hotels.

sections.heading: Absorbed by Concur
sections.body: TRX priced its IPO at $9 a share in September 2005 on the Nasdaq, below the $11 to $13 range it first planned. It spent several years as a small public company while it shifted toward travel data. In 2013 Concur, the travel and expense software maker, acquired TRX. Concur folded TRX's travel data tools into its own corporate travel products. SAP bought Concur the following year.

tagline: A Survivor of the Telecom Crash
dek: Eschelon gave small businesses in the West and Midwest one local provider for phones and internet.
lede: Eschelon Telecom filed to go public in 2005, after the telecom crash had wiped out many of its peers. It sold phone lines, internet access and phone systems to small and midsize businesses. It operated in cities across the West and Midwest, from Minneapolis to Seattle and Phoenix. In each of them, it competed with the large regional Bell company for the same customers.

sections.heading: Opened by the Telecom Act
sections.body: Eschelon began in 1996, soon after the Telecommunications Act opened local phone markets to competition. Its bet was that small businesses wanted one local provider with good service for all their communications. Eschelon leased parts of the incumbent's network instead of building every line itself. It bundled phone equipment with its lines. Like many competitive carriers of its era, it depended on access rules that regulators could change.

sections.heading: Bought by Integra
sections.body: Eschelon priced its IPO at $14 a share in August 2005 on the Nasdaq, below its planned range of $15 to $17. It grew through acquisitions of smaller carriers. In 2007 Integra Telecom bought Eschelon for about $710 million, including debt. The merger made Integra one of the largest competitive carriers in the western United States. The Eschelon name faded as its customers and networks moved into Integra.
